newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian president faces angry town over scandal.
newsitem.headline: Albanian president faces angry town over scandal.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha, seeking to shore up popular support, will explain his handling of collapsed pyramid investment schemes on Tuesday in this southern town, where angry investors rioted last month.
Officials said Berisha would travel to Lushnje, 85 km (53 miles) south of Tirana, in the afternoon to address a meeting of selected supporters of the ruling right-wing Democrats.
The theatre hall where Berisha will speak is next to the town hall, which was burned in January by protesters who had lost money in pyramid investment schemes.
A street-sweeper was cleaning the street in front the town hall and many official cars from Tirana could be seen around.
It will be the second time in four days that Berisha has tried to win support in the face of anti-government protests across the Balkan country.

The ruling Democrats also plans a mass rally in Tirana on Thursday to commemorate February 20, 1991, when protesters toppled the statue of communist dictator Enver Hoxha, who ruled Albania with an iron fist for 40 years.

Berisha is struggling to regain support for the free-market government which came to power in 1992 and which has faced protests and riots since the popular, but fraudulent, pyramid saving schemes collapsed last month.
Police have kept a tight grip in Tirana in recent weeks and broken up any opposition protests before they started.
Anti-government Lushnje protesters manhandled Deputy Prime Minister Tritan Shehu, beating him badly when he arrived at a stadium last month to discuss the scandal with angry investors.
About 3,000 anti-government demonstrators staged a 14th day of protests in the southern port of Vlore on Tuesday. Students have begun to join the daily rallies.
A banner proclaimed "Down with Berisha." Marchers chanted "Vlore is ours" and "We want our money back". Further back a group carried a giant Albanian flag.

In Tirana, Albania's last communist leader, Ramiz Alia, was charged with crimes against humanity and genocide. The trial was postponed after Alia's lawyer in the ramshackle courthouse demanded the judges resign because of procedural mistakes.
"The appeals court will rule on your request. I declare the session closed," presiding judge Martin Deda told Alia's lawyer Kleanthi Koci.
Ramiz Alia, 72, was the handpicked successor of Albania's Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha. Four other officials are also on trial, two in absentia.

The prosecutor accused the defendants of giving shoot-to-kill orders to border guards to stop Albanians from fleeing. If convicted, they face a mimimum penalty of 15 years and maximum of the death penalty.
In Tirana, scores of people queued outside the offices of two failed schemes, Populli and Xhaferri, expecting a partial reimbursement.

The government seized $300 in assets from the schemes and offered about 50 percent of clients' capital back. But Berisha has said no state money would be used to reimburse thousands of investors who lost everything.
Hundreds of depositors waited in muddy streets outside the offices of the Vefa Holding company, which froze the accounts of its 80,000 investors after the pyramid schemes collapsed.
Vefa insists it is solvent and will give investors their captial in three or four months, after the panic is over.
